templates.name: Main idea, informational study report (incl. explainer and scholar-argument passages)

items.passage: Leafhoppers, small sap-feeding insects, coat their bodies and wings with brochosomes, hollow particles that the insects secrete internally and then distribute over themselves with their legs. Each particle is pitted with holes about the size of a wavelength of light, and in 2017 mechanical engineer Tak-Sing Wong and colleagues found that this structure causes brochosomes to reflect very little of the light that strikes them, ultraviolet light included. Many of the birds and insects that prey on leafhoppers are capable of perceiving ultraviolet light.
items.stem: Based on the text, what is one advantage that brochosomes most likely provide leafhoppers?
options: They allow leafhoppers to detect the ultraviolet light reflected by approaching predators.
They make leafhoppers more difficult for some of their predators to see.
They conceal leafhoppers from predators by matching the ultraviolet patterns reflected by the leaves on which the insects feed.
They let leafhoppers absorb more light than other sap-feeding insects can, which keeps the insects warm in cool weather.
items.explanation: The text says that brochosomes reflect very little light, including ultraviolet light, and that many of the animals that hunt leafhoppers can perceive ultraviolet light. Putting those two facts together, a coating that reflects little of the light these predators see most likely makes leafhoppers harder for them to spot.

A.why_wrong: The text says the predators can see ultraviolet light; it says nothing about leafhoppers using brochosomes to detect light reflected by predators.

C.why_wrong: The text explains that brochosomes reflect very little light; it never says they reproduce any pattern reflected by leaves.

D.why_wrong: The text never compares leafhoppers with other sap-feeding insects or mentions body temperature.

sources.what: Penn State 2017: Tak-Sing Wong's team made synthetic brochosomes; leafhopper brochosomes are antireflective and likely camouflage against predators (Nature Communications)

items.notes: Natural science (entomology, materials). Premise 1: brochosomes reflect little light, UV included; premise 2: predators see UV; unstated conclusion: camouflage.

band7.why: Two premises (low reflectance including UV, predators see UV) and one unstated conclusion, with no definition or aside to map through; options 12 to 19 words; distractors are a twisted detail, a wrong mechanism and an invented comparison, and only C is partly right (concealment). A strong band 6.

items.passage: In Japan, silent films were seldom shown in silence during the 1910s and 1920s. Benshi, live narrators stationed beside the screen, voiced every character and supplied commentary of their own, and many moviegoers selected a theater on the strength of its benshi rather than its film; the most celebrated narrators were greater celebrities than the actors on the screen. Although sound films had largely supplanted silent ones in the United States by about 1930, Japanese studios continued releasing silent films well into that decade.
items.stem: Based on the text, why did Japanese studios most likely continue to release silent films into the 1930s?
options: Japanese audiences preferred films with little spoken dialogue because they found benshi commentary distracting.
Films narrated by benshi had begun to draw larger audiences in the United States than sound films did.
Actors in Japanese films had not yet been trained to perform dialogue for recorded sound.
Many filmgoers valued a part of the moviegoing experience that sound films would have made unnecessary.
items.explanation: The text says that many Japanese moviegoers selected a theater for its benshi rather than its film and that the best benshi were greater celebrities than the actors. Since a sound film carries its own voices, it would have left no role for the narrators audiences valued, which most likely explains why studios kept releasing silent films.

A.why_wrong: Audiences chose theaters because of the benshi, so they did not find the narrators distracting.

B.why_wrong: The text describes benshi only in Japan and never compares their audiences with audiences for sound films in the United States.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how Japanese actors were trained.

sources.what: Benshi: live narrators of Japanese silent film, often bigger stars than the actors; their popularity delayed the transition to sound, silent films made into the 1930s

items.notes: Arts and humanities (film history). Key abstracts the benshi into 'a part of the moviegoing experience'.

band7.why: Two statements plus one unstated link (sound would make the narrator redundant); the key abstracts the benshi into "a part of the moviegoing experience", but options run 14 to 18 words and the distractors (contradiction, invented comparison, unsupported) are each killed by one fact. A strong band 6.

items.passage: Shown how to open a box through a sequence that includes steps plainly irrelevant to the task, young children tend to reproduce every step, a behavior known as overimitation. Because the behavior had been documented only among children in affluent, industrialized societies, where adults often teach young children through explicit demonstration, psychologist Mark Nielsen and communication scholar Keyan Tomaselli compared children in Brisbane, Australia, with children in a remote San community in South Africa’s Kalahari Desert. The two groups copied the irrelevant steps at similar rates.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about overimitation?
options: It is likely more widespread among children than the earlier research had indicated.
It likely arises because children in both communities are taught to follow adults’ instructions without question.
It was likely more pronounced among the children in the Kalahari community than among those in Brisbane.
It likely fades once children are old enough to recognize which steps of a task are necessary.
items.explanation: Before Nielsen and Tomaselli’s study, overimitation had been documented only in affluent, industrialized societies. Their finding that children in a remote San community copied the irrelevant steps as often as children in Brisbane suggests that the behavior is not confined to such societies, so it is likely more widespread than the earlier research indicated.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how children in either community are taught to treat adults’ instructions.

C.why_wrong: The text says the two groups copied the irrelevant steps at similar rates, not that the Kalahari children did so more.

D.why_wrong: The text never discusses how overimitation changes as children grow older.

sources.what: Nielsen and Tomaselli 2010, Psychological Science 21:729-736, Overimitation in Kalahari Bushman children and the origins of human cultural cognition

items.notes: Social science (developmental psychology). The paper calls the community Bushman; the passage uses San. Box task kept general (no invented details of the irrelevant actions).

band7.why: One-step inference from "documented only among" plus "similar rates"; all four options hedged with "likely" in one frame, which is band-7-like, but none of the distractors is partly right (wrong mechanism, contradiction, unsupported). A strong band 6.

items.passage:
The following text is from María Amparo Ruiz de Burton’s 1885 novel The Squatter and the Don. Mercedes is in love with Clarence, who has just departed from a railway station on a westbound train. Mercedes remains at the station, anticipating the arrival of an eastbound train.

Two shrieks pierced the air simultaneously, as the two trains passed each other. Her heart gave accelerated throbs when she heard those shrieks, because she knew that one of them came from the train which bore Clarence away, and it seemed to her as if expressive of his pain at being torn from her. Yes, that magician, the locomotive, understood it all, and shrieked to say he did so, because he knew she, too, wished to shriek like that.
items.stem: Based on the text, how does Mercedes most likely feel as the trains pass each other?
options: She is alarmed, fearing that the shrieks are warnings that the two trains are in danger of colliding.
She is comforted, believing that the shriek of Clarence’s train is a sign that he will soon come back to the station for her.
She is anguished, imagining that the train expresses a sorrow at parting that Clarence shares with her.
She is embarrassed, worrying that the other travelers at the station can see how upset she is.
items.explanation: Mercedes’s heart races at the shrieks because one comes from the train carrying Clarence away, and the shriek seems to her to express “his pain at being torn from her.” The text adds that she “wished to shriek like that” herself, so she is anguished and imagines that Clarence feels the same sorrow at parting.

A.why_wrong: The shrieks are the trains’ whistles as they pass; Mercedes’s racing heart comes from thinking of Clarence, not from fear of a collision.

B.why_wrong: Mercedes hears the shriek as an expression of Clarence’s pain at leaving, not as a sign that he will return.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about other travelers or about Mercedes worrying what anyone sees.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of The Squatter and the Don (1885), chapter on the parting at the station; excerpt copied exactly, first sentence of the paragraph trimmed

items.notes: Literary prose, 1885 (published under the pseudonym C. Loyal). Context: Clarence leaves on the west-bound train; Mercedes waits for the east-bound one.

band7.why: Literary inference without irony: the key paraphrases the text's own "his pain at being torn from her"; distractors are a literal misreading, a twisted detail and an unsupported worry, each ruled out by one line. Band 6.

items.passage: Porous asphalt, common on Dutch highways because it drains rainwater quickly, gradually loses stones from its surface as tiny cracks form in its bitumen, the tarlike binder that holds the stones in place. Erik Schlangen, a materials scientist at Delft University of Technology, has engineered a version laced with fine steel fibers; when a machine heats the fibers by induction, the surrounding bitumen softens and flows into the cracks, sealing them. Schlangen concedes that “self-healing” overstates the material’s independent capabilities, but his team’s tests suggest that periodic heating could substantially prolong a road’s service life.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: An asphalt developed by Schlangen cannot repair itself unaided, but heating can seal its small cracks, which could make roads built with it last much longer.
Schlangen’s asphalt seals its own cracks without any outside help, which is why he considers it a truly self-healing material.
Because its steel fibers hold the stones firmly in place, Schlangen’s asphalt does not develop the tiny cracks that damage ordinary porous asphalt.
Although porous asphalt drains rainwater more quickly than other road surfaces do, induction heating has made it more costly to maintain than those surfaces.
items.explanation: The text explains that Schlangen’s asphalt contains steel fibers that, when heated by a machine, soften the surrounding bitumen so it seals cracks. It adds his own caution that the material is not truly “self-healing” and his team’s finding that periodic heating could greatly extend a road’s life. Choice A carries both the concession and the finding.

B.why_wrong: Schlangen says that “self-healing” overstates what the material can do on its own, since the repair depends on a machine.

C.why_wrong: The fibers do not prevent cracks; heating them softens the bitumen so that it flows into cracks that have formed.

D.why_wrong: The text never compares porous asphalt with other road surfaces or discusses maintenance costs.

sources.what: Schlangen's induction-healing porous asphalt with steel wool, Delft; tested on the A58; Schlangen says it is not really self-healing since it needs a machine

items.notes: Technology and engineering. Explainer build: phenomenon, mechanism, concession plus outlook.

band7.why: Two-part key carrying the concession and the finding, with a good CON, TWI, CMP mix, but options 20 to 26 words against the band-7 main-idea median of 34, and the correction rests on a plain "concedes", not a stance word to weigh. A strong band 6.

items.passage: Historians long described Tokugawa Japan (1603–1868) as sakoku, a “closed country” that cut nearly all ties with the outside world after the shogunate expelled Portuguese traders and forbade Japanese subjects to travel abroad in the 1630s. Historian Ronald Toby, however, showed that the shogunate conducted active diplomacy with Korea and the Ryukyu kingdom, receiving their embassies with elaborate ceremony, while Chinese and Dutch merchants continued to trade at Nagasaki. The term sakoku itself was coined only in 1801, by a translator rendering a European traveler’s account of Japan.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Toby argues that the restrictions the shogunate imposed in the 1630s had been largely abandoned by the time the term sakoku was coined in 1801.
Historians described Tokugawa Japan as a closed country mainly because they relied on a European traveler’s account that had been poorly translated.
Although Tokugawa Japan has often been characterized as a closed country, Toby’s research shows that it kept up significant diplomatic and commercial ties abroad.
Although the shogunate welcomed embassies from Korea and the Ryukyu kingdom, it refused to allow any merchants from outside Asia to trade in Japan.
items.explanation: The text opens with the long-standing view of Tokugawa Japan as a “closed country” and then turns, with “however,” to Toby’s evidence of active diplomacy with Korea and the Ryukyu kingdom and continuing trade with Chinese and Dutch merchants. Its last sentence notes that the label itself came late. Choice C states the old view and the correction.

A.why_wrong: The text never says the 1630s restrictions were abandoned; it shows only that Japan kept some foreign ties despite them.

B.recipe: invented cause for the old view
B.why_wrong: The text says the term was coined by a translator in 1801, but it does not say the translation was poor or that historians’ view rested on it.

D.why_wrong: Dutch merchants, who came from outside Asia, continued to trade at Nagasaki.

sources.what: Ronald Toby, State and Diplomacy in Early Modern Japan (1984): Tokugawa isolation far less complete than supposed; diplomacy with Korea and Ryukyu

items.notes: History (historiography). Sakoku coined by Shizuki Tadao in 1801 translating Kaempfer; translator left unnamed.

band7.why: Plain "however" correction rather than a stance word or litotes; only the key uses the "Although" frame; options 22 to 25 words; distractors are unsupported, an invented cause and a contradiction. A strong band 6.

items.passage:
The following text is Sarojini Naidu’s 1905 poem “Past and Future.” A hermit is someone who lives in deliberate solitude, withdrawn from society.

The new hath come and now the old retires:
And so the past becomes a mountain-cell,
Where lone, apart, old hermit-memories dwell
In consecrated calm, forgotten yet
Of the keen heart that hastens to forget
Old longings in fulfilling new desires.

And now the Soul stands in a vague, intense
Expectancy and anguish of suspense,
On the dim chamber-threshold . . . lo! he sees
Like a strange, fated bride as yet unknown,
His timid future shrinking there alone,
Beneath her marriage-veil of mysteries.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A soul that has grown weary of new desires withdraws to a quiet place where it can live among its memories.
A soul looks back with regret on the longings it once had and hesitates to accept a future in which new desires will replace them.
A bride who has not yet met her future husband waits anxiously behind her veil for the wedding to begin.
Having set aside its past for new desires, a soul faces a future it cannot yet know with both eagerness and dread.
items.explanation: In the first stanza the past becomes a remote “mountain-cell” of forgotten memories, left behind by a heart that “hastens to forget” old longings for new desires. In the second, the Soul waits in “expectancy and anguish” before a future that is “as yet unknown,” pictured as a veiled bride. Choice D states this movement from a forgotten past to an uncertain future.

A.why_wrong: In the poem the memories, not the soul, dwell apart like hermits; the soul turns toward new desires rather than away from them.

B.why_wrong: The heart “hastens to forget” its old longings, so the poem does not show regret for them.

C.why_wrong: The bride is a figure for the soul’s unknown future, not an actual bride awaiting a wedding.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Sarojini Naidu, The Golden Threshold (Heinemann, 1905), poem Past and Future; copied exactly (first line set in capitals in the source, given here in sentence case)

items.notes: Poem, 1905, extended figure (past as a hermit's cell, future as a veiled bride). Not used in any official item or ours.

band7.why: Two extended figures (hermit-cell past, veiled-bride future) must be carried into a general claim, which is the band-7 poem move, but each distractor falls to one line (literal bride, memories not the soul withdraw, "hastens to forget" rules out regret) and options run 20 to 25 words. A strong band 6.

items.passage: In Lake Tanganyika in eastern Africa, the cichlid fish Neolamprologus pulcher lives in groups in which a dominant breeding pair is assisted by subordinate “helpers” that defend the territory and clean the eggs. To investigate why helpers labor on behalf of offspring that are not their own, biologist Sigal Balshine-Earn and colleagues temporarily removed some helpers from their groups. When the helpers were reintroduced, other group members attacked them, and several were eventually expelled. Those that remained subsequently defended the territory and tended the young more diligently than before.
items.stem: According to the text, what happened after the helpers were returned to their groups?
options: They were welcomed back by the breeding pair but did less work than before.
They were attacked by other group members, and those that remained worked harder for the group.
They left their groups in order to form breeding pairs and territories of their own.
They avoided the breeding pair until the pair’s eggs had hatched.
items.explanation: The text says that when the helpers were reintroduced, other group members attacked them and several were expelled, and that the helpers that remained then defended the territory and tended the young more diligently than before. Choice B restates both parts.

A.why_wrong: The returned helpers were attacked, and those that stayed did more work, not less.

C.why_wrong: Several helpers were expelled by the group; the text does not say any left to start breeding on their own.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about helpers avoiding the breeding pair or about when the eggs hatched.

sources.what: Balshine-Earn, Neat, Reid and Taborsky 1998, Behavioral Ecology: helpers temporarily removed were attacked on return, some evicted, and returning helpers increased territory defence and brood care (pay to stay)

items.passage: After a failed Polish uprising in 1863, the Russian authorities who governed Warsaw restricted the teaching of Polish history and language, and the city’s university did not admit women. Beginning in 1882, Polish educators responded by holding secret courses for women in private homes, and in 1885 these courses were combined into a single underground institution later known as the Flying University. Its students paid small fees, which covered the teachers’ wages and even a modest library, and thousands of people eventually studied there.
items.stem: What does the text indicate about the Flying University?
options: It was established by Russian officials who wanted to expand the education available to Polish students in Warsaw.
Its courses met in public buildings that the authorities did not control.
It charged fees so high that only wealthy families could afford to attend.
It gave women in Warsaw access to an education that the city’s university denied them.
items.explanation: The text says that Warsaw’s university did not admit women and that Polish educators began holding secret courses for women, which in 1885 became the Flying University. So the institution offered women an education they could not get at the university.

A.why_wrong: The courses were organized in secret by Polish educators in response to restrictions imposed by the Russian authorities.

B.why_wrong: The courses were held in private homes, not public buildings.

C.why_wrong: The text says students paid small fees.

sources.what: Flying University: secret courses for women in private homes in Russian-ruled Warsaw from 1882, combined into one underground institution in 1885; small fees paid teachers and a library

items.notes: History (education). Marie Curie, a former student, left out as famous trivia.

items.passage:
The following text is from Grazia Deledda’s 1902 novel After the Divorce (translated by Maria Hornor Lansdale in 1905). Costantino has been sentenced to prison, where Don Serafino works as a guard. A group of officials has just inspected Costantino’s cell.

The party moved on, but before long Don Serafino returned and informed the prisoner that his term of solitary confinement had been shortened by more than a third, and that he would soon be released from his cell. Costantino supposed that he owed this favour to his good behaviour, but Don Serafino explained that it was because he had interceded for him with the authorities, telling them that the prisoner was of good family, that one of his feet had been flayed, and that he could make shoes.
items.stem: According to the text, why was Costantino’s term of solitary confinement shortened?
options: Don Serafino had spoken to the authorities on Costantino’s behalf.
Costantino had behaved well while he was confined to his cell.
The prison needed more workers who knew how to make shoes.
Costantino’s injured foot required care that he could not receive in his cell.
items.explanation: Don Serafino tells Costantino that his solitary confinement has been shortened because he “had interceded for him with the authorities,” telling them about Costantino’s family, his injured foot, and his skill at making shoes. Choice A states this reason.

B.recipe: contradicts the text (the first guess the text rejects)
B.why_wrong: Costantino assumes his good behavior earned the favor, but Don Serafino corrects him.

C.why_wrong: Shoemaking is one of the things Don Serafino mentioned to the authorities; the text does not say the prison needed shoemakers.

D.why_wrong: The flayed foot is part of what Don Serafino told the authorities; the text does not say Costantino needed treatment for it.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Grazia Deledda, After the Divorce, translated by Maria Hornor Lansdale (Henry Holt, 1905); original Dopo il divorzio, 1902; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Literary prose, translation. Don Serafino is the Neapolitan guard Costantino calls Uncle Serafino earlier in the chapter.

items.passage: The black palm Astrocaryum standleyanum produces seeds so large that they were probably once dispersed by enormous mammals that have since gone extinct, which raises the question of how the palm spreads its seeds today. On Barro Colorado Island in Panama, ecologist Patrick Jansen and colleagues attached miniature radio transmitters to hundreds of the seeds and monitored their movements. Agoutis, rabbit-sized rodents, buried most of the seeds. But rather than simply consuming them later, the agoutis repeatedly excavated and reburied the seeds, frequently stealing from one another, so that many seeds ultimately traveled more than 100 meters from their starting points.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Agoutis eat most of the black palm seeds they bury, which explains why the palm has become rare on Barro Colorado Island.
By tracking palm seeds with radio transmitters, researchers found that extinct mammals once carried the seeds more than 100 meters.
The agoutis’ habit of repeatedly digging up and reburying seeds may help explain how a palm once dispersed by now-extinct mammals still spreads its seeds.
Agoutis bury black palm seeds closer to the parent trees than the extinct mammals did, which limits how far the palm can spread.
items.explanation: The text asks how a palm whose large seeds were probably spread by now-extinct mammals disperses its seeds today, and it answers with Jansen’s tracking study: agoutis repeatedly excavated and reburied the seeds, moving many more than 100 meters. Choice C joins the question and the finding.

A.why_wrong: The agoutis repeatedly reburied the seeds instead of simply eating them, and the text never says the palm has become rare.

B.why_wrong: The transmitters tracked seeds moved by agoutis today, not by the extinct mammals.

D.why_wrong: The text never compares how far agoutis and the extinct mammals moved the seeds.

sources.what: Jansen et al. 2012, PNAS 109:12610-12615, Thieving rodents as substitute dispersers of megafaunal seeds (radio-tagged Astrocaryum standleyanum seeds, Barro Colorado Island)

items.passage: The Calusa, who dominated southwest Florida when Spanish explorers arrived in the 1500s, sustained a powerful kingdom without farming, relying instead on the fish and shellfish of the region’s estuaries. At Mound Key, the Calusa capital, archaeologist Victor Thompson and colleagues examined two large enclosures with walls built of shell, known as watercourts, that open onto a central canal. Sediments from inside the enclosures dating to the period of their use contained many fish scales, which were absent from the surrounding bay. The team concluded that the watercourts were used to hold live fish until they were needed.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The Calusa raised fish from eggs inside walled enclosures because the bay near Mound Key held few fish.
Archaeologists have found evidence that the Calusa built enclosures at their capital to store live fish for later use.
Fish scales from the bay near Mound Key show that the Calusa caught more fish than any other people in Florida.
The Calusa began farming once the fish kept in their watercourts were no longer enough to feed the people of the kingdom.
items.explanation: The text describes the Calusa as relying on fish rather than farming and then reports that Thompson’s team found fish scales in sediments inside the shell-walled watercourts at Mound Key, leading them to conclude that the enclosures held live fish until needed. Choice B states that conclusion.

A.why_wrong: The text says the enclosures held live fish until needed; it never says the Calusa raised fish from eggs or that the bay lacked fish.

C.why_wrong: The fish scales were found inside the enclosures, not in the bay, and the text compares the Calusa with no other group.

D.why_wrong: The text says the Calusa sustained their kingdom without farming.

sources.what: Thompson, Marquardt et al. 2020, PNAS 117, Ancient engineering of fish capture and storage in southwest Florida (Mound Key watercourts; fish scales inside, none in the bay)

items.notes: Archaeology. Paper is 2020 (PNAS); the passage gives no year.

items.passage: Hopi-Tewa potter Nampeyo (circa 1859–1942), who lived on First Mesa in northeastern Arizona, found inspiration in pottery made centuries earlier at Sikyátki, an abandoned village nearby. Studying fragments of these vessels, she took up their sweeping bird and feather motifs and their low, wide shapes, but rather than simply copying particular designs, she reworked them into compositions of her own. Her pots sold widely, and the style she developed was carried on by her daughters and by many later Hopi potters.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Nampeyo drew on an ancient local pottery tradition to create original work that influenced later potters.
Nampeyo reproduced the designs on Sikyátki vessels exactly so that the village’s pottery would not be forgotten.
Nampeyo’s pottery sold widely, but other Hopi potters rarely adopted the style she developed.
Nampeyo became known for pots that were taller and narrower than the vessels made at Sikyátki.
items.explanation: The text says Nampeyo took motifs and shapes from centuries-old Sikyátki pottery but reworked them into her own compositions, and that her style was carried on by her daughters and many later Hopi potters. Choice A generalizes these points.

B.why_wrong: Nampeyo reworked the old motifs into compositions of her own rather than simply copying particular designs, and the text gives no such purpose.

C.why_wrong: Her style was carried on by her daughters and many later Hopi potters.

D.why_wrong: She adopted the low, wide shapes of the Sikyátki vessels.

sources.what: Nampeyo (c. 1859-1942), Hopi-Tewa potter of First Mesa, founder of the Sikyatki Revival, drawing on ancient Sikyatki pottery without simply copying it

items.notes: Arts (profile).

fixes: passage: "rather than copying particular designs" became "rather than simply copying particular designs" (Wikipedia, Nampeyo: she began by copying Sikyatki designs and later developed her own style); why_wrong for B adjusted

items.passage:
The following text is from Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson’s 1860 novel A Happy Boy (translated by Rasmus B. Anderson in 1881). Oyvind, an exceptionally diligent student, expected to be ranked first among the adolescents preparing for confirmation in his church, but his school-master, convinced that Oyvind had studied merely out of vanity, arranged for him to be ranked lower.

The school-master waited for Oyvind until the latter had gathered together his books, then said that he would accompany him home. They walked slowly along. At first Oyvind was silent and his struggle went on, but gradually he gained his self-control. He was convinced that what had occurred was the best thing that in any way could have happened to him; and before he reached home, his belief in this had become so strong that he gave thanks to his God, and told the school-master so.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Oyvind hides his anger from the school-master because he is afraid of being ranked even lower.
Oyvind resolves to study even harder so that he can regain the rank he expected.
After an inner struggle, Oyvind comes to believe that his disappointment was for his own good.
The school-master walks Oyvind home in order to apologize for the decision he made.
items.explanation: At first Oyvind is silent and still struggling, but he gradually gains self-control and becomes convinced that what happened was “the best thing” for him, so firmly that he gives thanks and tells the school-master. Choice C states this change.

A.why_wrong: Oyvind’s silence is an inner struggle that ends in acceptance, not hidden anger, and nothing suggests he fears a lower rank.

B.why_wrong: The text says Oyvind comes to accept what happened; it says nothing about a plan to regain his rank.

D.why_wrong: The school-master accompanies Oyvind home, but the text does not say he regrets his decision or apologizes.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Bjornson, A Happy Boy, translated by Rasmus B. Anderson (author's edition, translator's preface dated November 1881); original En glad Gut, 1860; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Literary prose, translation. Context from the preceding scene: the school-master says Oyvind studied from vanity and that he had him put down.

items.passage: Kiwi are small, flightless birds found only in New Zealand, and scientists long assumed that their closest relatives were the emus and cassowaries of nearby Australia. In 2014, however, Kieren Mitchell, Alan Cooper, and colleagues analyzed DNA from the bones of elephant birds, enormous flightless birds of Madagascar that died out several centuries ago, and found that these birds were the kiwi’s closest relatives. The two lineages split about 50 million years ago, after New Zealand and Madagascar had already separated from each other and from other landmasses.
items.stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the common ancestor of kiwi and elephant birds?
options: It lived in Australia alongside the ancestors of emus and cassowaries.
It was larger than either of the birds that descended from it.
It died out before New Zealand and Madagascar separated from other landmasses.
It was capable of flight.
items.explanation: The kiwi and elephant birds are both flightless, yet their lineages split after New Zealand and Madagascar were already separated by ocean. For the two lineages to end up on islands that far apart, their common ancestor most likely could fly.

A.why_wrong: The text mentions Australia only in the assumption about the kiwi’s relatives that the DNA study overturned; it does not place the common ancestor there.

B.why_wrong: The text never gives or compares the size of the common ancestor.

C.why_wrong: The lineages split about 50 million years ago, after the landmasses had already separated, so the ancestor was still alive then.

sources.what: Mitchell, Cooper et al. 2014, Science: ancient DNA shows elephant birds and kiwi are sister taxa; split about 50 million years ago after landmasses separated, implying flighted ancestors

items.notes: Natural science (evolutionary biology). One-step inference: flightless descendants on islands separated before the split, so the ancestor flew.

items.passage: Sleep has generally been regarded as a function of the brain, since every animal known to sleep possessed a centralized nervous system. The upside-down jellyfish Cassiopea, however, lacks a brain, having only a diffuse network of nerves. Monitoring the jellyfish continuously, Caltech researchers Ravi Nath, Claire Bedbrook, and Michael Abrams found that the animals pulsed less frequently at night, responded more slowly to disturbances then, and were sluggish the following day if deprived of rest, all indications of a sleep-like state.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Cassiopea jellyfish sleep for longer periods each night than animals with centralized nervous systems do.
Although sleep has been linked to the brain, a jellyfish that has no brain appears to enter a sleep-like state.
Researchers found that Cassiopea develops a centralized nervous system as it matures, which is what enables the jellyfish to sleep.
Cassiopea jellyfish pulse less often at night because cooler water slows their movements.
items.explanation: The text begins with the view that sleep depends on the brain and then turns, with “however,” to Cassiopea, a jellyfish with no brain that shows signs of a sleep-like state. Choice B states both the earlier view and the finding that revises it.

A.why_wrong: The text never compares how long Cassiopea and animals with centralized nervous systems sleep.

C.why_wrong: The text says Cassiopea lacks a brain, having only a diffuse network of nerves.

D.why_wrong: The text presents the slower nighttime pulsing as a sign of sleep, not an effect of water temperature.

sources.what: Nath, Bedbrook, Abrams et al. 2017, Current Biology, The jellyfish Cassiopea exhibits a sleep-like state (nighttime quiescence, delayed response, reduced activity after deprivation)

items.notes: Natural science (neuroscience).

items.passage: The Ainu, an Indigenous people of northern Japan, have long passed down kamuy yukar, songs in which gods of nature narrate their own stories. In the early 1900s, government policies pressured the Ainu to abandon their language in favor of Japanese. Encouraged by the linguist Kindaichi Kyōsuke, a young Ainu woman named Chiri Yukie transcribed thirteen of these songs in Ainu, using the Roman alphabet, and translated them into Japanese. She died in 1922 at age nineteen, shortly after completing the manuscript, and the collection was published the following year.
items.stem: According to the text, what did Chiri Yukie do with the kamuy yukar?
options: She performed them for audiences in cities across Japan to share Ainu culture.
She changed them so that people, rather than gods, told the stories.
She wrote them down in the Ainu language and translated them into Japanese.
She translated them from Japanese into the Ainu language.
items.explanation: The text says that Chiri Yukie transcribed thirteen of the songs in Ainu, using the Roman alphabet, and translated them into Japanese. Choice C restates this.

A.why_wrong: The text says she transcribed and translated the songs; it never mentions performances.

B.why_wrong: In kamuy yukar the gods narrate their own stories, and the text does not say she changed that.

D.why_wrong: She wrote the songs in Ainu and translated them into Japanese, not the other way around.

sources.what: Chiri Yukie, Ainu Shin'yoshu (1923): thirteen kamuy yukar in romanized Ainu with Japanese translation, encouraged by Kindaichi Kyosuke; she died in 1922 at nineteen after finishing the proofs

items.notes: Humanities (literature, Indigenous language).

items.passage: For generations, Hmong women in Laos decorated clothing with paj ntaub, or “flower cloth,” a kind of needlework made up of geometric patterns rather than pictures. After the Vietnam War, many Hmong families fled to refugee camps in Thailand. There, beginning in the late 1970s, Hmong artists created story cloths, large embroidered panels showing scenes of village life and of their escape across the Mekong River. Because many families in the camps had little money, the artists sold the cloths to aid workers and visitors.
items.stem: According to the text, why did Hmong artists in the refugee camps sell story cloths?
options: To earn money that their families needed
To pay for materials for traditional flower cloth
To teach visitors about the history of the war
To raise money for a return trip to Laos
items.explanation: The text says that because many families in the camps had little money, the artists sold the story cloths to aid workers and visitors. Choice A gives this reason.

B.why_wrong: Flower cloth is the older needlework tradition; the text does not say the money went to materials for it.

C.why_wrong: The cloths show the escape across the Mekong, but the text gives the families’ need for money as the reason they were sold.

D.why_wrong: The text never mentions plans to return to Laos.

sources.what: Library of Congress blog (archived copy): first story cloths made at Ban Vinai refugee camp in Thailand from the late 1970s, showing escapes across the Mekong; they found a market outside the camps
La Crosse County Historical Society: in the Thai camps, with few chances of work, Hmong women made story cloths to sell to Western aid workers to earn income

items.notes: Arts (textiles). Options as 'To ...' fragments without a final period, as in 1.9.

fixes: sources: LOC blog URL now returns a database error; replaced with its archived copy (late 1970s, Ban Vinai, sold outside the camps) and added the La Crosse County Historical Society page that confirms the cloths were sold to aid workers to earn income

items.passage: On June 19, 1865, Union troops arrived in Galveston, Texas, and announced that all enslaved people in the state were free. Formerly enslaved Texans soon began commemorating the date annually with celebrations that became known as Juneteenth. In 1872, four formerly enslaved men in Houston, including the minister Jack Yates, raised $800 and purchased ten acres of land so that the city’s Black community would have a permanent location for the celebration. They named the site Emancipation Park, and it remains in use today.
items.stem: According to the text, why did Yates and the others buy the land?
options: To build a new church for Yates’s congregation
To provide a place for Union troops to camp
To create small farms for families who had recently been freed from slavery
To give the community a lasting site for Juneteenth celebrations
items.explanation: The text says the four men purchased the land so that Houston’s Black community would have a permanent location for the Juneteenth celebration. Choice D restates this reason.

A.why_wrong: Yates was a minister, but the text does not say the land was meant for a church.

B.why_wrong: Union troops appear in the text only as the ones who announced freedom in Galveston in 1865.

C.why_wrong: The text never says the land was used for farming.

sources.what: Emancipation Park, Houston: in 1872 Richard Allen, Richard Brock, Jack Yates and Elias Dibble bought 10 acres for $800 for Juneteenth celebrations

items.notes: History.

items.passage: Chankillo, a ceremonial site in coastal Peru constructed about 2,300 years ago, includes a row of thirteen stone towers along the crest of a low ridge. Archaeologist Iván Ghezzi and astronomer Clive Ruggles found that, viewed from an observation point west of the ridge, the row of towers spans the entire range of positions where the Sun rises throughout the year. As the seasons change, the sunrise shifts along the row from one end to the other. The researchers think the towers functioned as a calendar.
items.stem: According to the text, what do Ghezzi and Ruggles think the towers at Chankillo were used for?
options: Defending the site against attack
Keeping track of the time of year
Marking the graves of important leaders
Following the movements of the stars at night
items.explanation: The text says that the sunrise shifts along the row of towers as the seasons change and that Ghezzi and Ruggles think the towers functioned as a calendar. Choice B states that use.

A.why_wrong: The text never says the towers were used for defense.

C.why_wrong: The text does not mention graves or leaders.

D.why_wrong: The towers mark where the Sun rises, not the movements of the stars.

sources.what: Newswise release on Ghezzi and Ruggles 2007 (Science): the 13 towers of Chankillo, about 2,300 years old, mark the Sun's rising and setting through the year; "the oldest solar calendar" identified in the Americas

items.notes: Archaeology (archaeoastronomy).

fixes: sources: PUCP CRIS URL returns 404; replaced with the Newswise release on the 2007 Ghezzi and Ruggles Science paper

items.passage: Giant tortoises on the Galápagos Islands consume large quantities of fruit, swallowing the seeds whole. Ecologist Stephen Blake and his team investigated what happens to those seeds. They found that seeds can remain inside a tortoise for as long as four weeks. GPS trackers attached to tortoises showed that the animals can travel considerable distances in that time, especially during seasonal migrations between the islands’ lowlands and highlands. The researchers concluded that the tortoises can carry seeds far from where they eat them.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Research shows that Galápagos tortoises can spread seeds far from the plants that produced them.
Galápagos tortoises eat fruit only when other kinds of food are hard to find.
Seeds that pass through Galápagos tortoises sprout faster than seeds that fall from plants.
GPS trackers show that Galápagos tortoises rarely travel far from where they feed.
items.explanation: The text explains that seeds can remain inside a tortoise for up to four weeks and that the tortoises can travel considerable distances in that time. It ends with the researchers’ conclusion that tortoises can carry seeds far from where they eat them, which choice A states.

B.why_wrong: The text says the tortoises consume large quantities of fruit; it never says they eat fruit only when other food is scarce.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how quickly any seeds sprout.

D.why_wrong: The GPS trackers showed that the tortoises can travel considerable distances.

sources.what: Blake et al. 2012, Journal of Biogeography, Seed dispersal by Galapagos tortoises (GPS telemetry and digesta retention, up to about four weeks)

items.notes: Natural science (ecology). Retention figure rounded from 6-28 days in the companion captive study.

items.passage: In 2012, a Swedish children’s book used the word hen, a pronoun that refers to a person without specifying whether that person is male or female. The word provoked a heated public debate. Psychologists Marie Gustafsson Sendén, Emma Bäck, and Anna Lindqvist repeatedly surveyed Swedish adults about hen between 2012 and 2015. In 2012, most respondents disliked the word, but by 2014, attitudes had become noticeably more positive. Participants also reported using hen more frequently, though this change was smaller than the shift in attitudes.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: By 2014, most Swedish adults had begun using hen in place of other pronouns.
The word hen was invented in 2012 by the author of a popular Swedish children’s book.
Swedish adults who disliked hen in 2012 were still refusing to use the word three years later.
Swedish attitudes toward a new pronoun became more positive within just a few years.
items.explanation: The text says that most Swedes disliked hen in 2012 but that by 2014 attitudes had become noticeably more positive, with use rising somewhat as well. Choice D states this main finding.

A.why_wrong: Use of hen increased, but the text says this change was smaller than the change in attitudes; it does not say most adults had begun using it.

B.why_wrong: The text says the book used the word in 2012, not that its author invented it.

C.why_wrong: Attitudes became more positive and use increased between 2012 and 2015.

sources.what: Gustafsson Senden, Back and Lindqvist 2015, Frontiers in Psychology 6:893: majority negative to hen in 2012, significant positive shift by 2014, use increased less than attitudes

items.notes: Social science (psychology of language).

items.passage:
The following text is from Amy Levy’s 1888 novel The Romance of a Shop. After their father’s death leaves them with little money, four sisters plan to support themselves by running a photography studio from their new home in London.

Then followed a period of absorbing and unremitting toil. All through the sweet June month the girls laboured at setting things in order in the new home. Expense being a matter of vital consequence, they endeavoured to do everything, within the limits of possibility, themselves. Workmen were of course needed for repairing the studio and fitting the kitchen fire-place, but their services were dispensed with in almost every other case.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The sisters miss their old home and find it hard to settle into the new one.
The sisters hire workmen to prepare their new home so that they can spend their time on the photography business.
The sisters work hard to prepare their new home, doing as much of the work as they can themselves.
The sisters spend the month of June searching for a home they can afford.
items.explanation: The text describes a month of “unremitting toil” in which the sisters set the new home in order and, to save money, did everything they could themselves, hiring workmen only for a few jobs. Choice C states this.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about the sisters missing their old home.

B.why_wrong: Workmen were used only for the studio and the kitchen fireplace; the sisters did almost everything else themselves.

D.why_wrong: In June the sisters were already setting things in order in the new home, not looking for one.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Amy Levy, The Romance of a Shop (T. Fisher Unwin, first published 1888); excerpt copied exactly (first four sentences of the paragraph)

items.notes: Literary prose, 1888. British spellings (laboured, endeavoured) kept as in the source.

items.passage:
The following text is from Alice Brown’s 1895 short story “Farmer Eli’s Vacation.” Eli, a farmer, has longed to see the ocean since childhood. Having finally traveled to the coast with his family, he accompanies his daughter onto some rocks overlooking the water.

Eli went; and when they had picked their way over sand and pools to a headland where the water thundered below, and salt spray dashed up in mist to their feet, he turned and looked at the sea. He faced it as a soul might face Almighty Greatness, only to be stricken blind thereafter; for his eyes filled painfully with slow, hot tears.
items.stem: Based on the text, how did Eli most likely feel when he looked at the sea?
options: He felt disappointed because the sea seemed smaller than he had imagined.
He felt awed because the sea seemed so vast and powerful to him.
He felt annoyed because the salt spray had gotten into his eyes.
He felt homesick because the sea reminded him of how far he was from his farm.
items.explanation: When Eli finally looks at the sea, he faces it “as a soul might face Almighty Greatness,” and his eyes fill with tears. These details suggest that he was deeply awed by the sight.

A.why_wrong: Eli faces the sea “as a soul might face Almighty Greatness,” which shows he found it immense, not disappointing.

C.why_wrong: The spray dashes up to his feet; his eyes fill with tears because of what he feels on seeing the sea.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about Eli thinking of his farm.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Alice Brown, Meadow-Grass: Tales of New England Life (Copeland and Day, 1895), story Farmer Eli's Vacation; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Literary prose, 1895. Context from the story: Eli has lived within driving distance of the ocean but never seen it and has long planned a trip to the shore.
